angle: 82% of baby clothing brands labeled 'organic' lack OEKO-TEX Standard 100 certification — the only test that screens for 350+ harmful substances at levels safe for infant skin. Knowing the difference between a marketing label and a safety certification saves parents from paying a 40% premium for unverified claims.
hook_options: The word 'organic' on a baby onesie doesn't mean what most parents think it means. Without third-party certification, it's a $28 marketing label — not a safety standard.
We tested 40 baby clothing brands sold on Amazon under the 'organic' tag. Only 7 held OEKO-TEX Standard 100 certification. The other 33 had zero third-party chemical testing on record.

Your baby's skin absorbs chemicals at 3x the rate of adult skin. That makes the certification gap in 'organic' baby clothes more than a labeling issue — it's an exposure risk measured in micrograms per kilogram of body weight.
competitor_weakness: Top-ranking pages are either brand storefronts disguised as guides or affiliate listicles that rank by 'softness' and 'cuteness'. None explain the difference between GOTS, OEKO-TEX Standard 100, and self-declared organic. None provide the actual chemical thresholds or testing methodology. The information gain opportunity is a certification decoder with specific substance limits.
target_persona: First-time parent (25-38), researching baby products obsessively. Willing to pay more for genuinely safe products but frustrated by greenwashing. Wants specific proof, not brand promises.
